1.q: Earth science is the study of:
1.a: Our planet and its neighbors in space
wrong: Only rocks, gems, minerals, and the soil on top
1.why: Earth science is the study of our planet and its neighbors in space.

1.q: What is the official name of the metric system?
1.why: Scientists everywhere use the metric system, officially called SI.

1.q: Which is the right order for the first three steps of the scientific method?
1.a: Observe, ask a question, make a hypothesis
wrong: Make a hypothesis, then observe, then conclude
1.why: The scientific method starts with observe, then ask a question, then make a hypothesis.

1.q: Which of these is a model?
wrong: A rock sample from a creek
1.why: A weather forecast is a computer model, and models help us see things we can't see directly.

1.q: Which unit fits best for recording a rock's mass?
1.why: In the metric system, mass is measured in grams and kilograms.

1.q: A friend says plate tectonics is "just a theory." What is the best reply?
1.a: In science, a theory is well tested and backed by evidence
wrong: True, a theory is just a wild guess with no testing
Theories only describe what happens, never why it happens
A theory can never change, so it is a proven fact forever
1.why: A scientific theory explains why something happens and is backed by tons of evidence and testing.

1.q: Why are metric conversions so easy?
1.a: Everything goes by tens, like 100 cm in a meter
wrong: Every unit is split into 12 parts
There is only one unit for everything
The units change from one country to the next country
1.why: In the metric system everything goes by tens, such as 100 centimeters in a meter.

1.q: A student measures mountain snow depth and creek height every week. Which step is this?
1.why: In the creek example, the experiment or gather-data step is to measure the snow and measure the creek.

1.q: You test whether slope angle changes how fast sand slides. What is the independent variable?
wrong: The kind of sand you use each time
The stopwatch you time it with
1.why: The independent variable is the thing you change on purpose.

1.q: You test if water temperature changes how fast salt dissolves. Which should be a control?
1.a: The amount of salt each time
1.why: Everything besides the independent variable stays the same as a control, so it's a fair test.

1.q: A pot of water starts to boil. About what does a Celsius thermometer read?
Your lab partner wants to taste a white mineral to see if it is salt. You should:
1.a: Stop them, because you never taste anything in lab
wrong: Let them try just a very small lick to check
Tell them to wait and taste it after class
Have them smell it up close instead of tasting
1.why: Lab safety rules say never taste anything in the lab.

2.q: A spot's latitude and longitude together are called its:
2.why: Put latitude and longitude together and you get coordinates, a spot's address.

2.q: What does a compass rose show on a map?
2.why: A compass rose shows north, south, east, and west.
Contour lines connect points at the same elevation, or height above sea level.

2.q: Which lines measure how far east or west you are?
2.why: Longitude lines measure how far east or west you are from the prime meridian.

2.q: The International Date Line sits near which longitude?
2.why: The International Date Line is out in the Pacific, near 180°.

2.q: Why is the Mercator projection still used, even though it distorts sizes?
wrong: It is the only round map
It keeps every shape and size
2.why: The Mercator projection is great for navigation but makes places near the poles look huge.

2.q: What does an equal-area projection give up to keep sizes correct?
2.why: Equal-area projections keep sizes correct but bend shapes.

2.q: Why do firefighters and search-and-rescue teams use topographic maps?
2.a: They show the land's shape, like cliffs and valleys
wrong: They show every street name and road number
They list the weather forecast for each day of the week
They show the time zones and the Date Line
2.why: A topographic map shows the shape of the land, its hills, valleys and cliffs, on a flat page.

2.q: About how many satellites make up the GPS system?
2.why: For GPS, about 30 satellites orbit Earth.

2.q: Trail A crosses widely spaced contour lines. Trail B crosses tightly packed ones. Which is the easier walk?
2.a: Trail A, since spread-out lines mean a gentle slope
wrong: Trail B, since tightly packed lines mean flatter ground
You can't tell from contour lines
2.why: Contour lines far apart mean a gentle slope, and close together means steep.

2.q: Earth turns 360° in 24 hours. How many degrees does it turn each hour?
2.why: Split 360° by 24 hours and you get 15° per hour.

2.q: Scientists want to watch a wildfire spread across central Idaho from above. Which tool fits best?
2.why: Remote sensing uses satellites and planes to photograph and scan Earth, which is how we track wildfires.

3.q: Where are protons and neutrons found in an atom?
3.why: Protons and neutrons are both in the center of the atom, the nucleus.

3.a: The force holding atoms together in a compound
wrong: A layer of rock deep in Earth's crust
A super-hot, electrically charged gas, like in lightning
A mix of a solid and a liquid together
3.why: The force that holds atoms together in a compound is called a chemical bond.

3.a: Water vapor cools into liquid droplets
wrong: Ice warms up and melts into liquid
Liquid water heats up into vapor
Lava cools down into solid rock
3.why: When water vapor cools and turns back into liquid droplets, that's condensation.

3.a: Atoms of different elements bond together
wrong: Atoms of one element sit by themselves
A solid melts and becomes a liquid
A gas spreads out to fill its container
3.why: When atoms of different elements bond together, they make a compound.

3.q: Table salt is a compound of:
3.why: Table salt is sodium plus chlorine.

3.q: What usually changes matter from one state to another?
3.a: Adding or removing energy, usually heat
wrong: Adding more atoms of the same element
Painting it or changing its color
Moving it to a new place on Earth
3.why: Adding or removing energy, usually heat, changes the state of matter.

3.q: Where does Earth's internal heat come from?
3.a: Heat left from Earth's formation plus radioactive decay
wrong: Sunlight soaking deep down into the ground every single day
Friction from ocean waves rubbing the crust
Lightning strikes that heat up the crust
3.why: Earth's internal heat is left over from when the planet formed, plus heat from radioactive elements breaking down.

3.q: Why can the water you drink today be very old?
3.a: Matter on Earth is recycled over and over in cycles
wrong: New water is made fresh inside clouds every single day
Water stays in one place once it forms
Water is created by plants as they grow
3.why: Matter on Earth gets recycled over and over, so the water you drink may once have been dinosaur sweat.

3.q: Why do Earth scientists call Earth a system?
3.a: Its parts are linked, so a change in one affects the rest
wrong: Each of its spheres works completely alone, with no links
It is made of only one kind of matter
It has stayed exactly the same over time
3.why: Change one part of the system, and the rest feel it.

3.q: A bowling ball and a beach ball are the same size. Which has more mass?
3.a: The bowling ball, because it has more matter
wrong: The beach ball, because it's lighter
They're equal because they're the same size
Neither one, since balls have no mass
3.why: Mass is how much matter something has, and a bowling ball has more than a beach ball of the same size.

3.q: Lava flowing out of a volcano is in which state of matter?
3.why: Liquids take the shape of their container, and water and lava are liquids.

3.q: A puddle disappears on a sunny afternoon. What happened to the water?
3.why: Adding heat makes liquid water evaporate into vapor.

4.why: Inorganic means not made by living things.

4.q: A mineral's crystal structure means its atoms:
4.a: Line up in a repeating pattern
wrong: Are always in a liquid state
4.why: Crystal structure means the atoms line up in a repeating pattern, like perfectly stacked blocks.

4.q: Calcite belongs to which mineral family?
4.why: Carbonates contain carbon and oxygen, and calcite is one.

4.q: Which mineral is number 9 on the Mohs scale and includes rubies and sapphires?
4.why: Corundum is number 9 on the Mohs scale and includes rubies and sapphires.

4.q: What does a gem have to be?
4.a: Rare, hard, and beautiful enough to cut
wrong: Soft enough to scratch with a fingernail
4.why: A gem is a mineral that's rare, hard, and beautiful enough to be cut and polished.

4.q: Why is diamond counted as a native element?
4.a: It is made of pure carbon
wrong: It is made of silicon and oxygen
It is a liquid deep underground
4.why: Native elements are pure elements found on their own, including diamond, which is pure carbon.

4.q: Why are seashells and pearls not true minerals?
4.a: Living things make them, so they aren't inorganic
wrong: They are much too soft and crumbly to count as minerals
They are made of liquid, not solid
They don't have any color or luster
4.why: A mineral must be inorganic, not made by living things, so seashells and pearls are close calls.

4.q: Why is quartz the same mineral no matter where it's found?
4.a: It has a definite recipe: silicon and oxygen
wrong: It always has exactly the same color
It only ever forms in Idaho's granite mountains
It is made by living things in the sea
4.why: A mineral has a definite chemical makeup, and quartz is always silicon and oxygen.

4.q: How does the Mohs scale rank its 10 minerals?
4.a: Each one scratches the minerals below it
wrong: By how shiny and bright each one looks
By how much each one costs to buy
By the color of the streak each leaves
4.why: On the Mohs scale, each mineral scratches the ones below it.

4.q: Which mineral is found in toothpaste?
A shiny gray mineral leaves a reddish-brown streak on a white tile. It is most likely:
4.why: Hematite can look silver or black, but its streak is always reddish-brown.

4.q: About how many minerals are known?
4.why: There are over 5,000 known minerals, but only about 20 or so are common.

5.q: The word "igneous" comes from the Latin word for:
5.why: The word igneous comes from the Latin word for fire.

5.a: The size, shape, and arrangement of crystals
wrong: How much silica and iron the rock holds inside it
How hot the magma once was
What color the rock looks in sunlight
5.why: Texture is the size, shape, and arrangement of the crystals.

5.q: Which of these is an intermediate igneous rock?
5.why: Intermediate igneous rocks are in between felsic and mafic, like andesite and diorite.

5.a: A giant chunk of granite in central Idaho
wrong: A lava tube at Craters of the Moon
Basalt layers under the Snake River Plain
5.why: The Idaho Batholith is a giant chunk of granite in central Idaho, including the Sawtooth Mountains.

5.q: Gabbro is which kind of igneous rock?
5.why: Mafic rocks are dark and rich in iron and magnesium, like basalt and gabbro.

5.q: Why does magma rise toward the surface?
5.a: It is lighter than the solid rock around it
wrong: It is heavier and denser than the rock around it
Wind on the surface pulls it upward
It freezes and expands like ice
5.why: Since magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, it rises like a blob in a lava lamp.

5.q: How does mafic lava behave compared with felsic magma?
5.a: It is runny and flows easily
5.why: Mafic lava is runny and flows easily, while felsic magma is thick and sticky.

5.q: Why did Native Americans make arrowheads from obsidian?
5.a: It is volcanic glass that chips to razor-sharp edges
wrong: It is soft enough to carve easily with just a fingernail
It floats, so arrows fly farther
It is full of big, strong crystals
5.why: Obsidian is natural volcanic glass, and Native Americans chipped it into razor-sharp arrowheads.

5.q: About how hot does it get where rock melts into magma?
5.why: Magma forms deep in the Earth where it's hot enough, roughly 700 °C to 1,300 °C, to melt rock.

5.q: A geologist finds a light-colored rock with big, easy-to-see crystals in the Sawtooths. It is most likely:
5.why: Granite is light-colored and coarse-grained, and the Sawtooth Mountains are part of the granite Idaho Batholith.

5.q: A dark rock with tiny crystals comes from a lava flow at Craters of the Moon. It is most likely:
5.why: Basalt is dark and fine-grained, and Craters of the Moon has fresh-looking basalt lava fields.

5.q: Which igneous rock is used in scrubs and stones for rough feet?
5.why: Pumice is used in exfoliating scrubs and pumice stones for rough feet.

6.q: Clastic sedimentary rocks are made from:
wrong: Minerals left behind as water evaporates
6.why: Clastic rocks are made from broken pieces of other rocks.
Clastic rocks are sorted by size, and shale is made of super-fine mud.
Non-foliated metamorphic rocks have no layers.

6.q: Old chalkboards and some roofs are made of which metamorphic rock?
6.why: Shale becomes slate, which was used for old chalkboards and roofs.

6.q: Why is metamorphism compared to baking cookie dough?
6.a: The rock changes but never melts
wrong: The rock melts and then hardens
The rock is glued by minerals
6.why: Metamorphism is like baking cookie dough: the rock changes but doesn't turn back into liquid.

6.q: Why are sedimentary rocks called history books?
6.a: Their layers hold clues like fossils
wrong: They are always the oldest rocks on Earth
They form when lava cools at the surface
They never change once they have formed
6.why: Sedimentary rocks form in layers that hold clues like ripple marks, mud cracks, and fossils.

6.q: Why can you see so much history in the Grand Canyon?
6.a: It's a stack of nearly 2 billion years of rock layers
wrong: It's one giant block of very old granite
It was carved out of one single, enormous ancient lava flow
It's made of metamorphic marble and gneiss
6.why: The Grand Canyon is a giant stack of sedimentary layers, nearly 2 billion years of history.

6.q: How long can it take for sediment to become rock?
wrong: A few hours to a few days
About one week to one month
6.why: Compaction and cementation can take thousands to millions of years.

6.q: A rock layer shows cracks shaped like a dried-up puddle. What does that suggest?
6.a: The area was once a lake that dried up
wrong: A volcano once erupted right there
It formed deep underground under pressure
A glacier once covered the whole area
6.why: Sedimentary rocks can hold clues like mud cracks from dried-up lakes.

6.q: Granite is squeezed deep in a mountain range until its minerals form striped bands. It becomes:
6.why: Granite turns into gneiss, a foliated rock with striped bands.

6.q: Some limestone is made of billions of tiny shells. What kind of sedimentary rock is that?
6.why: Organic sedimentary rock is made from the remains of living things, like limestone made of tiny shells.

7.q: About how long has Earth been running the rock cycle?
7.why: Earth has been running the rock cycle for about 4 billion years.

7.q: Which agents break rock into sediment?
7.a: Wind, water, ice, and plant roots
7.why: In weathering and erosion, wind, water, ice, and plant roots break rock into sediment and carry it away.

7.q: In the chapter's rock journey, which rock is metamorphic?
7.why: Heat and pressure turned buried sandstone into quartzite, a metamorphic rock.

7.q: Melting in the rock cycle needs:
7.why: In the rock cycle, heat deep underground turns rock into magma.

7.q: Why is the rock cycle more like a choose-your-own-adventure than a circle?
7.a: Rocks can skip steps, go backward, or take shortcuts
wrong: Every rock follows the exact same set path, step by step
Rocks can only move in one direction
Only igneous rocks are able to change
7.why: There's no set path: a rock can skip steps, go backward, or take shortcuts.

7.q: In the chapter's rock journey, how does granite become sand?
7.a: Rain, ice, and wind break it apart
wrong: It melts and then cools very quickly
Heat and pressure squeeze it deep down
It gets glued together on a lake bottom
7.why: The granite gets pushed up into mountains, and rain, ice, and wind break it into sand.

7.q: How does the biosphere play a part in the rock cycle?
7.a: Roots and living things help break rock down
wrong: Living things melt solid rock down into fresh magma
Animals push rock upward into mountains
Plants turn buried sand into quartzite
7.why: Roots and living things play a part, since plant roots help break rock into sediment.

7.q: A landslide moves tons of sediment in seconds. What does this show?
7.a: Some parts of the rock cycle can be fast
wrong: The whole rock cycle only ever takes a few seconds
Gravity has no role in the cycle
7.why: Most of the rock cycle is slow, but a landslide can move tons of sediment in seconds.

7.q: If weathering and erosion stopped, which rock type would stop forming?
7.why: Weathering and erosion make sediment, which is pressed and glued into sedimentary rock.

7.q: Broken basalt settles in layers on the bottom of an Idaho reservoir. What step turns it into rock?
wrong: Uplift and weathering at the surface
7.why: Sediment gets pressed and glued into sedimentary rock by compaction and cementation.

7.q: Rivers and glacier ice wearing down rock show which sphere at work in the rock cycle?
7.why: In the rock cycle, water and ice are part of the hydrosphere.

7.q: Metamorphic rock is pushed up into a mountain and weathers into sediment. Can that happen?
7.a: Yes, it can weather into sediment
wrong: No, metamorphic rock must melt first
No, only igneous rock can weather
Only after it turns into igneous rock
7.why: There's no set path, and metamorphic rock can weather into sediment.

8.a: Breaks rock without changing what it's made of
wrong: Changes minerals in the rock into brand-new substances
Carries rock pieces to new places
Melts rock deep underground into magma
8.why: Mechanical weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing what it's made of.

8.q: Over time, water turns the mineral feldspar into:
8.why: Water slowly dissolves some minerals and turns feldspar into clay.

8.q: The B horizon, or subsoil, is:
8.a: Lighter, with clay and minerals washed down
wrong: Dark and rich in humus from rotting plants
Fallen leaves and other decaying stuff
Solid rock at the very bottom of the hole
8.why: The B horizon is lighter, with clay and minerals washed down from above.

8.a: The top layer of fallen leaves and decay
wrong: Lighter soil full of washed-down clay
Solid rock at the very bottom
8.why: The O horizon is the top layer of fallen leaves and decaying stuff.

8.a: Weathered rock, humus, water, air, and life
wrong: Only sand, gravel, and small pebbles
Only rotting plants and dead animals
Cooled lava, volcanic ash, and pieces of obsidian glass
8.why: Soil is a mix of weathered rock, humus, water, air, and billions of living things.
Deposition builds deltas, sand dunes, and beaches.

8.q: Why is ordinary rainwater slightly acidic?
wrong: It picks up salt from the sea
8.why: Rainwater picks up carbon dioxide and becomes slightly acidic.

8.q: Why does frost wedging work so well in Idaho?
8.a: Temperatures swing above and below freezing
wrong: The climate there is always warm and wet
There are no plants there to block the ice
The rocks there have already rusted away
8.why: Frost wedging works best where temperatures swing above and below freezing, like here.

8.q: A handful of healthy soil has more living things in it than:
wrong: There are stars in the sky
There are grains of sand on a beach
There are drops in the ocean
8.why: A single handful of healthy soil has more living organisms in it than there are people on Earth.

8.q: If weathering is smashing a cookie, erosion is like:
8.why: Think of weathering as smashing a cookie and erosion as the ants carrying the crumbs away.

8.q: A huge rock dome has curved slabs peeling off like an onion. What process is this?
8.why: In unloading, rock on top erodes away and the rock below expands and peels off in sheets, like an onion.

8.q: Loose rocks lie in a pile at the bottom of a cliff after a rockfall. Which agent moved them?
8.why: Gravity pulls everything downhill, causing landslides and rockfalls.

9.q: About how fast does creep move?
9.why: Creep is super slow, maybe a few centimeters a year.

9.a: Water-soaked soil flowing like a thick milkshake
wrong: Rocks breaking off a high cliff and free-falling down
Sand slowly walking downwind in a desert
A huge mass of ice moving slowly over land
9.why: In a mudflow, soil soaked with water flows like a thick milkshake.

9.a: Forms in mountains and flows down valleys
wrong: Covers most of a continent like a sheet
Forms in hot, dry deserts near the equator
Is a giant pile of windblown sand
9.why: Valley glaciers form in mountains and flow down valleys, like slow-motion rivers.

9.a: Wind-blown sand blasting and polishing rock
wrong: Wind piling up fine dust into thick, fertile layers
9.why: Wind-blown sand blasts and polishes rocks, like nature's sandpaper.

9.q: Rocks break off a cliff and free-fall onto the road below. This is a:
9.why: In a rockfall, rocks break off a cliff and free-fall.

9.q: About how long ago did glaciers cover much of North America?
9.why: About 20,000 years ago, during the last ice age, glaciers covered much of North America.

9.q: Why does water help trigger mass movement?
9.a: It adds weight and makes soil slippery
wrong: It freezes the soil solid and locks it in place
It removes weight from the slope
It makes plant roots grow faster
9.why: Water adds weight and makes soil slippery.

9.q: How do glaciers carve the land?
9.a: They pluck up rocks and grind them along the bottom
wrong: They melt the rock beneath them into magma
They blow sand against cliffs to polish them
They dissolve limestone with weak acid as they move along
9.why: As glaciers move, they pluck up rocks and grind them along the bottom, scratching and carving the land.

9.q: If all of Antarctica's ice melted, sea level would rise about:
9.why: If Antarctica's ice all melted, sea level would rise about 58 meters (190 feet).

9.q: A road crew cuts into a steep hillside to widen a highway. What risk goes up?
9.why: Cutting into hillsides for roads and houses can trigger mass movement.

9.q: Wind can't lift big rocks. What is it best at moving?
9.why: Wind can't lift big rocks, but it's great at moving sand and dust.

9.q: During an earthquake, a big mass of rock and soil suddenly breaks loose and races downhill. This is a:
9.why: A landslide is a big mass of rock and soil that suddenly breaks loose and races downhill; earthquakes can trigger it.

10.why: Precipitation is water falling as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.

10.a: Flows over the ground into streams
wrong: Soaks deep down into the soil
Rises into the air as water vapor
10.why: In runoff, water flows over the ground into streams.

10.a: Slower, wider, and starting to curve
wrong: Fast, steep, and cutting down hard
Cut off into a curved pond
10.why: Mature rivers are slower, wider, and start to curve.

10.q: In Idaho, the Continental Divide runs along:
10.why: The Continental Divide runs along the Idaho-Montana border.

10.q: Why was nearly every town in history built next to a river?
10.a: People survive only about three days without water
wrong: Rivers keep towns much cooler during the hot summer months
River water never floods its banks
Rivers block wind, dust, and storms
10.why: You can last weeks without food but only about three days without water, so towns grew next to rivers.

10.q: About how much water poured out when the Teton Dam failed?
10.why: When the Teton Dam failed, about 80 billion gallons of water poured out.

10.q: Why is Bear Lake, on the Idaho-Utah border, turquoise?
10.a: Tiny bits of limestone float in the water
wrong: Copper ore lines the whole lake floor
Algae paint the water a bright blue
Glacier ice still floats on its surface
10.why: Bear Lake's turquoise color comes from tiny bits of limestone floating in the water.

10.q: About how much of Earth's water is frozen in ice?
10.why: About 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean water and about 2% is frozen in ice.

10.q: A town wants flood control that also filters pollution and helps wildlife. What is its best choice?
10.why: Wetlands filter pollution, prevent floods, and provide homes for wildlife.

10.q: Near its source, a river has rapids, waterfalls, and a deep V-shaped canyon. This part of the river is:
10.why: Young rivers near the source are fast and steep and carve deep V-shaped valleys, rapids, and waterfalls.

10.q: Which Idaho town was flooded when the Teton Dam failed?
10.why: When the Teton Dam failed in 1976, water flooded Rexburg, Sugar City, and other towns.

10.q: A family wants to build a new house. Why should they avoid the floodplain?
10.a: The river spills onto it when it overflows
wrong: It is too far from any source of drinking water
The soil there is too poor for a yard
It stays frozen solid every winter
10.why: When more water enters a river than its channel can hold, it spills onto the floodplain, so it's a dangerous place to build.

11.a: Where groundwater flows out on its own
wrong: A hole that is drilled to pump water up
A layer of clay that blocks groundwater
The very top of the zone of saturation
11.why: A spring is where groundwater naturally flows out at the surface.

11.a: A hole drilled below the water table
wrong: A cave formed by acidic water
11.why: A well is a hole drilled below the water table so water can be pumped up.

11.a: The upper layer where spaces hold air and some water
wrong: The lower layer where every single space is full of water
A layer of clay that blocks water
The very top of an aquifer
11.why: The zone of aeration is the upper layer, where spaces hold both air and some water.

11.a: Build up from the floor toward the ceiling
wrong: Hang down tight from the ceiling like icicles
Form when the roof of a cave falls in
Shoot out hot water and steam
11.why: Stalactites hang tight to the ceiling, and stalagmites might reach the ceiling someday.

11.q: Old Faithful in Yellowstone erupts about every:
11.why: Old Faithful erupts about every 90 minutes on average.

11.q: Why does the water table's depth change?
11.a: It rises in wet times and drops in droughts
wrong: It moves up and down with the ocean tides
It follows the phases of the Moon each month
It stays at the same depth all year
11.why: The water table's depth changes with the seasons, rising in wet times and dropping in droughts.

11.q: What does Idaho have more of than almost any other state?
11.why: Idaho has more soakable hot springs than almost any other state.

11.q: Compared with all rivers and lakes, how much fresh liquid water is underground?
11.why: There's about 30 times more fresh liquid water underground than in all the rivers and lakes on Earth.

11.q: Why is an aquifer more like a soaked sponge than an underground lake?
11.a: Water fills spaces in permeable rock
wrong: It is one huge open cave full of water
It is a frozen block of underground ice
It only holds water on its top surface
11.why: An aquifer is a layer of permeable rock or sediment that holds and moves groundwater, like a soaked sponge.

11.q: A septic tank leaks near a family's well. Why is that a worry?
11.a: Pollution can soak down into the groundwater
wrong: It will change the well into a gushing artesian well
It will raise the water table safely
It will turn the well into a geyser
11.why: Pollution from leaky septic tanks can soak down into aquifers.

11.q: You drill a hole but stop above the water table. What will you likely get?
11.a: Little water, since spaces there hold air too
wrong: A strong gush of water rising up with no pump at all
Hot water heated by nearby magma
More water than any deeper well
11.why: Above the water table is the zone of aeration, where spaces hold both air and some water.

11.q: Water entering the Eastern Snake River Plain Aquifer may take how long to travel through it?
wrong: About one month or a little more
11.why: Some of the water takes decades or even centuries to travel through the aquifer.

12.a: An instrument that records seismic waves
wrong: A map that shows all of Earth's layers
A drill used to dig very deep holes
A compass that tracks magnetic fields
12.why: Scientists record seismic waves with instruments called seismographs.

12.q: About how much of Earth's volume is the mantle?
12.why: The mantle makes up about 84% of Earth's volume.

12.q: How do P waves move rock?
12.a: They squeeze and stretch it, like a pushed Slinky
wrong: They shake it side to side, like a flicked rope
They melt it as they pass
12.why: P waves squeeze and stretch rock, like a Slinky pushed from one end.

12.q: About how thick is oceanic crust?
12.why: Oceanic crust is thin, about 7 km.

12.q: Earth's inner core is about as hot as:
12.why: The inner core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, around 5,200 °C.

12.q: Why did drillers stop the Kola Superdeep Borehole?
12.a: The rock was so hot it acted like putty
wrong: They broke through into the liquid outer core
They drilled all the way into the ocean
